newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-HEAT IS ON FOR RULE CHANGES AT OPEN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HEAT IS ON FOR RULE CHANGES AT OPEN.

text.p: Pete Sampras thought his feet were on fire, Goran Ivanesevic's legs went numb and the women just did not want to play.
The heat was on from players past and present at the Australian Open on Monday for the rule book to be updated, as Melbourne sizzled in a heat wave.
Sampras, who survived a five-set battle with little-known Slovak Dominik Hrbaty, feared that officials would only take action after someone had become seriously ill.

"I think there's going to have to come a point where someone really gets hurt out there to make some sort of rule (change)," he said after almost losing to 19-year-old Hrbaty in a match lasting nearly three hours.
The mercury topped 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit) on the court for a second consecutive day at Melbourne Park.
On Sunday Belgian 16th seed Sabine Appelmans had to be placed on an intravenous drip and world number one Steffi Graf was treated for heat exhaustion.
Five-times grand slam champion John Newcombe called for the introduction of a 10-minute break at the end of the third set.
Sampras said: "Part of me is saying, sure, it would be nice to have a break ... but as an athlete you should be in good enough condition to go out (and) play in any condition."
"But the quality of the tennis in this heat is not going to be great," he said.
Gerald Segal of the Australian Medical Association said: "It could be just a matter of time before someone dies out there."
Under women's rules, play can be delayed in extreme conditions, but a bid by players to postpone their matches on Monday was over-ruled by the committee which runs grand slam tournaments.

"They said it's not fair for the other players who played yesterday, and for the moment they don't have this rule," said Romanian eighth seed Irina Spirlea after her fourth round victory over ninth seed Karina Habsudova of Slovakia.
Their match was delayed by 30 minutes as grand slam officials reviewed their request.
"We were just asking if it's possible to play tomorrow," Spirlea said.
In men's tennis there are no rules governing extreme heat.
Cooling fans were placed beside the courts and players draped ice-packed towels over their shoulders at the change of ends and drank carbonated "hydro-fuel" in a bid to cool down.
"It was so hot today, it was a joke," said Sampras, adding the Rebound Ace surface absorbed the heat and made it tougher to breathe and play.
"My feet were on fire and we were both feeling it."
Third-seeded Ivanisevic said he was forced to concede several points during his three-hour-and-four minute battle with Norway's Christian Ruud.
"You cannot try the whole game, otherwise you die; after 10 minutes you're dead," the big-hitting Croat told reporters after his five-set duel.
"I didn't feel too much in my legs ... I was out of it, I didn't know where I was."
A relieved Ivanisevic fell to his knees after his long battle in front of a handful of supporters on an outside court, but bounced straight back up.
"That was a mistake ... I was almost burned, but I was so tired I had to fall down."
